newsitem.title: USA: Telecoms pact must stand test of time - U.S. industry.
newsitem.headline: Telecoms pact must stand test of time - U.S. industry.

text.p: U.S. telecom companies hailed a ground-breaking pact to open most of the world's $600 billion telecommunications market, but industry analysts were more cautious, saying benefits would be longer-term.

"This global pact holds much promise for deregulated markets and offers huge opportunities, but we must be careful not to expect too much, too soon," said Jeffrey Kagan, an industry analyst at Kagan Telecommunications Association.
Under the auspices of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), 68 countries meeting in Geneva clinched a deal to bring free-trade principles to the telecom industry.

U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky hailed the trade agreement, saying it would open new markets for U.S. firms, lower costs for consumers and double or triple the size of the $600-billion-a-year industry over the decade.
But while a slew of U.S. companies praised the pact, telecommunications specialist Kagan warned that concrete benefits could be a while in coming.
"It is a global version of what we did last year with the Telecommunications Act of 1996," Kagan said.

The U.S. Telecommunications Act of 1996, enacted on February 8, ended decades of legal barriers and encouraged domestic local and long-distance carriers, cable-TV operators, electric utilities and others to invade each other's backyards in terms of offering services.
But some industry analysts say that one year later, the act has drummed up more hype than competition.
Kagan said: "The devil is in the details, and for a while, the only ones making money will be the lawyers."
Two other analysts also said they needed more time to study the details of the pact.
This pact on basic telecoms will for the first time bring services such as satellite systems, cellular phones, data transmission and paging under the WTO.
Barshefsky said before the pact, only 17 percent of the top telecom markets were open to U.S. companies. Now, U.S. companies would have access to nearly 100 percent of those markets.
Big companies with international clout, like AT&T Corp, MCI Communications Corp, British Telecommunications plc, Sprint Corp and BellSouth Corp would benefit first, Kagan said.
"We might also see some more alliances with natural partners, like the UK, Germany and France," he said.

U.S. call-back services, which let customers make international phone calls via another country with cheaper charges, might benefit in the short term, but would lose popularity over time as telephone rates dropped, Kagan said.
AT&T welcomed the pact, saying it would like to see telecommunications markets in other countries become as open as the United States.
But AT&T spokeswoman Susan Fleming also said the pact would probably not dramatically alter the company's strategy, because it already was and would remain active abroad.
"I don't think one agreement is going to make us change our course," she said. "Certainly, this agreement helps but it doesn't necessarily change our strategy."
AT&T also said it did not expect heightened competition at home to pose a threat to the company.
Foreign firms would have trouble luring U.S. callers away from their domestic telephone service providers, Kagan said.

MCI said it would work with the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to develop regulatory safeguards to ensure that the U.S. industry could compete effectively at home while taking advantage of opportunities abroad.
Sprint said it was excited by the opportunities the pact offered, in that more than 60 of the most important coutnries committed to open their telecommunications market.
